items.followUp: Define electron affinity and state its commonly used unit.

rubric.why: This identifies the process and the gaseous atom to which the definition applies.
rubric.description: States that ionization energy is required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential definition of removing an electron from an isolated gaseous atom.

rubric.why: A correct unit completes the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct unit, such as kJ mol⁻¹ or eV per atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct unit.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy is the energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom to form a positive ion.
Its unit is kJ mol⁻¹ (or eV per atom).

items.followUp: What is meant by a polar covalent bond?

rubric.why: Equal sharing of the bonding electrons is the defining feature of a non-polar covalent bond.
rubric.description: States that the bonded atoms share the electron pair equally.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for equal sharing of electrons.

rubric.why: Equal sharing means there is no separation of charge across the bond.
rubric.description: States that the bond has no positive and negative poles (no charge separation).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the absence of poles or charge separation.

modelAnswer: A non-polar covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the bonded atoms share the electron pair equally.
As a result, no positive and negative poles are formed.

items.followUp: Define crystalline solids and give one example.

rubric.why: Amorphous solids lack the regular, ordered arrangement found in crystalline solids.
rubric.description: States that the particles have no regular long-range arrangement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the irregular arrangement of particles.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates recognition of an amorphous solid.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as glass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: Amorphous solids are solids whose particles do not have a regular long-range arrangement.
Glass is an example of an amorphous solid.

items.followUp: Name two factors that affect the rate at which a solid solute dissolves in a liquid.

rubric.why: Any one valid factor earns the first mark.
rubric.description: Names one factor affecting solubility, such as temperature, pressure, or the nature of the solute and solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid factor.

rubric.why: A second distinct valid factor earns the second mark.
rubric.description: Names a second distinct factor affecting solubility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second valid factor; do not award both marks for repeating the same factor.

modelAnswer: Two factors that affect solubility are temperature and the nature of the solute and solvent.

items.followUp: Write two chemical properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Metals commonly form oxides with oxygen, react with water to release hydrogen, or react with acids to form a salt and hydrogen.
rubric.description: Gives one correct chemical reaction or property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid property, such as formation of metal oxide with oxygen or reaction with an acid to release hydrogen.

rubric.why: A second distinct property is required for the second mark.
rubric.description: Gives a second correct chemical reaction or property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct valid property.

modelAnswer: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides.
Many metals react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen gas.

items.followUp: What are noble gases? State the group in which they are found.

rubric.why: Halogens are located in Group 17 of the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct group.

rubric.why: Halogens are reactive non-metals known as salt-formers.
rubric.description: Describes halogens as reactive non-metals or salt-formers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct description.

modelAnswer: Halogens are the reactive non-metal elements of Group 17 of the periodic table.

items.followUp: Define covalent compounds and state three of their properties.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds consist of oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction, usually following electron transfer.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic compound as one made of positive and negative ions held by electrostatic attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, including ions and their electrostatic attraction.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds typically form crystalline solids.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds are crystalline solids (or hard and brittle).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct physical property.

rubric.why: Strong electrostatic attraction between ions requires considerable energy to overcome.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds have high melting or boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct melting-point or boiling-point property.

rubric.why: Ions can move and carry charge in molten or aqueous compounds, but not in the solid state.
rubric.description: States a correct electrical-conductivity property of ionic compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for conductivity when molten or aqueous, or lack of conductivity as a solid.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are compounds made of positive and negative ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
They have high melting and boiling points.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

items.followUp: Describe applications of isotopes in medicine, agriculture and industry.

rubric.why: Radioisotopes have important medical uses, including cancer treatment and diagnosis or treatment of thyroid disorders.
rubric.description: Gives a correct medical application of an isotope.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for a correct isotope and its medical use.

rubric.why: Isotopes can trace nutrient uptake in plants, while radiation is used in food preservation and crop improvement.
rubric.description: Gives a correct agricultural application of isotopes or radiation.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for a correct agricultural application, preferably identifying the use and relevant isotope or process.

rubric.why: Radioisotopes are used in industry to inspect materials or locate leaks in pipelines.
rubric.description: Gives one correct industrial application of an isotope.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct industrial use.

modelAnswer: In medicine, cobalt-60 is used in the treatment of cancer; iodine-131 is used to diagnose or treat thyroid disorders.
In agriculture, phosphorus-32 is used as a tracer to study the absorption of phosphate by plants; radiation can also be used to preserve food.
In industry, radioisotopes such as sodium-24 can be used to detect leaks in pipelines.
